messages.text: I don’t know why I’m even texting you. Everything just feels pointless.

It sounds like you’re feeling overwhelmed and maybe hopeless right now. I’m glad you reached out—those feelings can be heavy to carry alone. Can you tell me more about what’s been making things feel pointless for you?
I’m not glad I reached out—I’m just desperate. There’s a difference.

I hear you, and that difference matters. Desperation can feel raw and urgent, and it often comes from a place of deep pain. Would you feel okay describing what’s been happening recently that brought you to this point?
I’ve been thinking about death a lot. I don’t fear dying—it’s the opposite, almost. I wish I could just… fade out peacefully. The thought of being buried and rotting scares me more than death itself.

It sounds like you’ve been having frequent thoughts about wanting life to end, and that can be very serious. I want to make sure you’re safe—are you currently thinking about ending your life, or making any plans to harm yourself? Your safety matters, and if you’re at risk, it’s important to get immediate support. Would you be willing to talk about what happens when these thoughts get strongest?

I’m not making plans. I just… don’t see the point in going on like this. Being around people exhausts me, and being alone feels like drowning. It’s not about wanting to hurt myself—it’s about wanting the weight to stop.

It sounds like you’re feeling trapped between exhaustion and isolation, with no space that feels peaceful. That constant heaviness can be deeply draining. We could explore what’s been adding to that weight, and what small shifts might make things feel more manageable. Would you like to focus on what’s been most overwhelming lately or on moments when things feel a bit less heavy?
Everything just feels heavy all the time. Even small things take too much effort. I can’t remember the last time I felt light, or hopeful, or even curious about anything.

Feeling that constant heaviness and lack of hope can be signs that your mind and body are deeply depleted. When nothing feels light, it’s hard to imagine change, but small steps can slowly shift that weight. Sometimes starting with basic needs—like rest, nourishment, or gentle movement—can make more space for relief. Would you be open to exploring one tiny, manageable thing you could try for yourself today?
I know you’re trying to help, but “tiny steps” feel pointless when the whole thing is broken. I’m not saying no—I’m just saying it doesn’t feel like it would change anything.

I understand—it’s hard to believe small actions matter when the bigger picture feels shattered. Sometimes, those steps aren’t about fixing everything right away, but about giving you brief moments of relief to make the next moment more bearable. You don’t have to commit—just noticing what feels even slightly less heavy can be a start. Would you like me to help you identify what those moments might look like for you?
Part of me wants to feel better. But another part just doesn’t believe anything will help. I’ve tried so many things—it all just circles back to this.

It sounds like you’re caught between wanting change and feeling hopeless because past efforts haven’t lasted. That can make it really hard to trust the process or even try again. Sometimes the focus shifts from “fixing everything” to finding ways to hold steady in the hardest moments. Would you like to talk about what has helped you cope, even briefly, in the past?
What helped before doesn’t work anymore. I’m not the same person I was back then. I can’t just reuse old tricks when everything feels different now.

It makes sense that strategies from before might not fit who you are or what you’re facing now. When things change, the ways we cope sometimes have to evolve too. We can explore new approaches that match where you are today, without expecting you to go back to who you were. Would you be willing to try identifying one need you have right now that feels unmet?
I don’t have the energy to try new things. Even thinking about it feels exhausting. I just want to not feel this heavy for once.

It’s understandable that the idea of trying feels overwhelming when your energy is so low. Sometimes the first step can be simply allowing yourself to rest without pressure to change. In moments like this, focusing on very gentle, passive forms of comfort—like listening to calming sounds or sitting in a quiet space—might ease the heaviness slightly. Would you like me to suggest a few low-effort ways to create that kind of space?
I’ve tried all that—music, quiet, breathing. It doesn’t help. It just… passes time.

It sounds like those activities feel more like distractions than true relief, and that can be frustrating. Sometimes the heaviness needs more connection or support than solitary coping can provide. Talking with someone who can hold that weight with you—like a friend, therapist, or crisis counselor—might feel different. Would you consider reaching out to someone in your life or a helpline so you’re not carrying this alone tonight?
I don’t want to talk to a stranger. I’m not in crisis—I’m just tired. Tired of pretending I’m okay when I’m not.

You’re being honest here about how hard it is to keep pretending, and that honesty matters. Even if you’re not in crisis, sharing your real feelings with someone you trust could relieve some of that tiring weight. Sometimes we need spaces where we don’t have to act “okay” at all. Is there anyone in your life you feel safe being completely honest with right now?
The only person I can be honest with is my dad, and even then I hold back. I feel so alone.

Feeling alone, even with someone you trust, can be deeply isolating. It might help to gently let your dad know more about what you’re carrying, so you don’t have to hold back as much. You don’t have to tell him everything at once—small, honest pieces can open space for support. Would you like help thinking through how to start that conversation with him?
I can’t burden him with this. He’s already worried. I don’t want to make it worse.

It’s natural to want to protect him, especially if you feel he’s already worried. Sometimes sharing can feel like burdening, but it can also give loved ones a chance to truly be there for you. You can choose how much to share, focusing on letting him know you’re struggling without going into every detail. Would you feel more comfortable expressing that you need support in a way that feels safe for both of you?
I do want him to know I’m struggling… but I’m scared of how he’ll take it. He’s all I have. I can’t risk losing that.

It’s clear how important your relationship with your dad is, and that makes your fear of his reaction understandable. You might frame it gently, focusing on how his presence helps you rather than on the depth of your pain. This can signal that you’re struggling while reassuring him his role matters. Would you like me to help you put that into words you could feel safe saying?
Maybe. I just don’t know if words would even help. They never have before.

It’s okay to feel uncertain about whether words will make a difference, especially if past attempts haven’t helped. Sometimes the act of speaking is less about fixing and more about opening a door between you and someone who cares. Even a small, honest sentence can be a step toward feeling less alone. Would you like to try crafting something short that you might say or write to him?
I don’t know… talking hasn’t fixed anything, but it hasn’t made it worse either. That’s something, I guess.

That’s true—sometimes the value is in keeping the connection alive, even if it doesn’t solve everything right away. It shows you’re not fully shutting yourself off, and that can matter more than it seems. Maybe sharing just enough so he knows you’re hurting could be a gentle way forward. Would you like me to suggest a simple sentence you could use with him?
I’ll think about it. I don’t need a script. I just need to know it’s okay to not be okay.

It is absolutely okay to not be okay, and you don’t have to hide that truth. Struggling doesn’t make you weak—it shows you’re human and carrying more than one person should have to alone. You deserve support and compassion, even in the heaviest moments. Would you like to focus now on ways to be kinder to yourself while you’re feeling this way?
I’m tired. Can we stop for tonight?
Of course. You’ve shared a lot, and it’s okay to rest now. I’m still here whenever you want to talk again. I hope you can find even a small moment of comfort tonight.
